slides.title: The residual stream
slides.summary: Each layer reads the token vectors, works something out and adds the result back. Information builds up instead of being replaced.
body: The most helpful way to picture a transformer: a wide stream of vectors, one per token, flows from the bottom of the model to the top.
Each layer has two parts: attention and an MLP. Each part reads the stream, works out an update, and adds it back: x = x + f(x). Nothing is replaced. Updates pile up.

ul: Why it helps training: learning sends an error signal backwards through every layer. The simple addition gives that signal a shortcut to the earliest layers, so even 100-layer models train reliably. This is called a residual or skip connection.
Why it helps the model think: each layer can make a small, focused edit, like adding "this word is a verb" or "this refers to Paris", which later layers can read.

body.note: Picture a shared document that every layer adds notes to. Nobody deletes earlier notes; each layer writes its own in the margin, and the final reader sees them all at once.

code: x = x + self.attn(self.norm1(x))   # read, write back

figure.alt: The residual stream of token vectors flows from left to right. First a normalised copy goes through attention and the result is added back to the stream. Then another normalised copy goes through the MLP and that result is added back. The shape stays n by d throughout, and the block is repeated N times with its own weights.
figure.caption: Every block in every LLM follows this pattern. The rest of this chapter looks at each part.

slides.title: Normalisation: keeping numbers steady
slides.summary: Before each part of a layer, vectors are rescaled to a standard size so the numbers stay stable.
body: Every layer adds to the stream, so the numbers can keep growing on the way up. Big, jumpy numbers make training unstable.

So just before each attention or MLP part, a copy of the vector is normalised to a standard size. Only the copy going in is rescaled; the stream keeps its values. Doing it at this point is called pre-norm, and it's standard in modern LLMs. There are two common ways:

ul: LayerNorm: subtract the average, divide by how spread out the numbers are (the standard deviation), then apply a learned scale and shift.
RMSNorm: skip the average and just divide by the typical size of the numbers (the root-mean-square). Slightly cheaper, works just as well, and used by Llama and many others.

body: Try it: make the input ten times bigger. <mark>The normalised output doesn't change at all.</mark>

body.note: Normalisation keeps the input to each part in a predictable range, however much has built up in the stream. It's a small step, but deep models don't train well without it.

slides.title: The MLP: where most of the parameters are
slides.summary: The MLP works on each token by itself. It holds most of the model's parameters and a lot of what it knows.
body: Attention moves information between tokens. The MLP (multi-layer perceptron, also called the feed-forward network) then works on each token by itself, in three steps:

ul: Expand: multiply the vector up to a much wider size, usually about 4 × d.
Bend: pass every number through a simple curved function (shown on the right).
Shrink back: multiply back down to size d, ready to add to the stream.

body: <mark>About two-thirds of a model's parameters are in these MLPs.</mark> Research suggests they partly work like a memory for facts: a pattern meaning "Eiffel Tower" in the input switches on parts of the MLP that add "Paris" to the stream.

Two matrix multiplications in a row are the same as one. Without a bend in between, the whole model would collapse into one simple straight-line function, however many layers it had. The curved activation function is what lets stacked layers learn complicated patterns. Modern models use smooth curves like GELU or SiLU, often in a form called SwiGLU.
code: def forward(self, x):          # x: [B, n, d]
return self.w2(h)                     # back to [B, n, d]

slides.title: Count the parameters yourself
slides.summary: You can estimate a model's size, and how much memory it needs, from three numbers.
body: Each layer's weights come from a few matrices, so the number of parameters is easy to estimate:

ul: Attention: four d × d matrices (Wq, Wk, Wv, Wo) = 4d².
So each layer has about 12d², and the whole model has about 12·N·d², plus V·d for the embedding table.

body.note: A 7B-size model has d = 4,096 and N = 32 layers: 12 × 32 × 4,096² ≈ 6.4 billion, plus about 0.1 billion for a 32k-token embedding table. Real designs differ a little (GQA, SwiGLU's three matrices), but the estimate comes out close.

body: Each parameter is stored as a fixed-size number: 2 bytes in bf16 (the usual format), 1 byte at 8 bits, or half a byte in 4-bit quantised formats. A 7B model needs about 14 GB in bf16 but only about 3.5 GB at 4 bits. That's how quantisation lets big models run on a laptop.
Try the presets, then move the sliders.

body.note: That's only the weights. Running the model also needs memory for the KV cache (see Output & inference), and training needs several times more for the extra numbers it keeps track of.

code: params = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())
# 7B params * 2 bytes = ~14 GB just to load in bf16

slides.title: Stack it N times
slides.summary: A model is the same layer design repeated many times, each copy with its own weights.
body: A full model is one block repeated N times: 32 layers for a typical 7–8B model, 80 or more for the biggest open models. Every block has the same design, but each has its own learned weights.
Research into model internals finds rough patterns in what different layers do:

ul: Early layers: simple, local patterns, like word pieces joining up into words.
Middle layers: more abstract ideas, like topic, meaning and how things relate.
Late layers: turning all of that into a guess for the next token.

body: These are general trends, not strict rules.

body.note: Because every block takes [B, n, d] in and gives [B, n, d] out, the number of layers is just a setting. The main dials are width (d), depth (N) and number of heads (h). Making a model bigger mostly means turning these up.

slides.title: Mixture of experts
slides.summary: Mixture-of-experts models have many MLPs per layer but only use a few for each token. So they're huge, but fairly cheap to run.
body: Many top models replace each layer's single MLP with a group of experts: several separate MLPs, plus a small router. For each token, the router picks the best few experts (often 2, sometimes 8 out of more than 100) and mixes their outputs.

ul: The benefit: the total number of parameters, and so how much the model can know, grows a lot. But each token only goes through a few experts, so the work per token stays small.
The cost: every expert has to be kept in GPU memory, even when it's not being used.
The catch: the router has to be trained to share the work evenly. Otherwise it sends everything to a few favourites and the rest are wasted.

body: Pick different tokens on the right to see different experts light up.

body.note: "Expert" is a misleading name. Experts don't neatly specialise in subjects like "maths" or "French". What they actually specialise in is usually much harder for people to make sense of.

code: out = sum(w[..., i] * experts[idx[..., i]](x) for i in range(2))
